title: Huawei's Ascend chose the hardest road: not compatible with Nvidia
dek: For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that does not solve a choke point but instead goes proactively into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder the longer you do it.
why: The first half is about how the book was written, with low information density; from the two key decisions at Ascend's project launch onward, Fang Xingdong gives a lot of frontline detail and judgment that only appear in the book.
who: Founders, investors and engineers watching domestic compute, the semiconductor supply chain and AI infrastructure, especially those who want to understand the difference between Ascend's and Nvidia's routes.
skip: The first ~13 minutes cover the origin and interview process of the six books, with little relevance to investment judgment.

points.h: Ascend's toughest decision was not being compatible with Nvidia
points.body: At project launch Ascend faced two choices. The first was whether AI chips should be specialized or general-purpose; Liao Heng, as chief scientist, judged that AI should be a general-purpose product, and the architectural choice has proven correct today. The second was harder: whether to be compatible with Nvidia. Many domestic chips chose compatibility, with the benefit that Nvidia's existing ecosystem and tools could be shared. But Xu Zhijun was firm from the start that they must take a different path. Fang Xingdong believes this choice was extremely bold at the time, and that they faced enormous challenges many times along the way — because the entire Chinese IT industry has been a follower industry for three or four decades, and had never developed based on its own root technologies.

points.h: Anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder
points.body: Fang Xingdong recalls having dinner with Xu Zhijun three years ago, when Xu half-muttered to himself: Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets harder and harder. There are two kinds of following: in standardized products, Chinese companies can always catch up and even overtake, but by the time they overtake there is little profit left in the industry — 2G to 5G, PCs, phones all went this way; in non-standardized areas, such as competing with Cisco in routers for so many years, they have not gotten closer. In Xu Zhijun's eyes, what Huawei did in the past was also following. So Ascend is special among the six products: the other five solve choke points and address survival first, while Ascend was not choked in 2019 — it is a fully proactive compute product.

points.h: With process choked off, only system innovation can make it back
points.body: Industry chips gain roughly 20%+ performance per generation, mainly from increased transistor counts driven by advanced process improvements. Huawei lost this premise and can only gain performance through system innovation and breakthroughs — stacked compute, interconnect, higher integration. Fang Xingdong uses a car metaphor: previously you just made the engine stronger and stronger, but now the engine is constrained and cannot be enlarged, so you can only make the car run well through architecture, weight reduction, heat dissipation and other factors. Nvidia's solution is to keep working on the engine, because TSMC can still manufacture for it. In the interview Liao Heng uses the metaphor of an 18-story pagoda: many companies are good at only one layer because of the great division of labor, while Huawei is forced to do manufacturing, ecosystem and chip design all at once.

points.h: Huawei has to bring the domestic supply chain up with it
points.body: Previously Huawei did design, relied on the global supply chain, had TSMC manufacture, could choose the best international partners for other components, directly buy American products and assemble them, sell at a good price with brand premium and decent profit. Now it cannot cooperate with foreign partners, TSMC cannot process for it, and domestic processes are still lacking in every respect, so Huawei has no choice but to support and drive the domestic supply chain — only then does it have a way to survive and get products manufactured. So the challenge of the past seven years is not just improving its own capabilities but also driving the entire supply chain — without driving it, independent autonomy is impossible. Manufacturing is not Huawei's main business, but it has to help companies like SMIC and Yangtze Memory continuously advance process, yield and quality.

points.h: Ascend's significance is not Huawei surviving, but the industry having an engine
points.body: In the past Huawei's product launches and iterations were still based on American root technologies and industrial ecosystem; the high-value components of a phone were basically foreign. Now Huawei's phones, including Ascend, drive almost 100% domestic supply chains. Fang Xingdong believes the greatest significance of the Tao Law is not that Huawei itself can survive and be autonomous, but that China's entire semiconductor industry and entire IT industry have their own engine, which never existed before. Huawei's rapid development represents the rapid development of the entire industrial ecosystem. He also points out that the market, looking at reports, news or public opinion, has not yet realized that we are at this inflection point — when Nvidia is mentioned people think it is formidable, when Huawei is mentioned they say it is policy that makes people use it.

points.h: It is not a question of difficulty, but of cognition and determination
points.body: Fang Xingdong believes doing communications versus doing IT is essentially not a question of difficulty but of cognition and determination — whether you dare to do it. The most typical example is the Gauss database: among the six products Ascend stood out, and the least conspicuous may be Gauss, but databases are a half-century-old industry with a relatively stable market, and if truly choked it would be deadly. At the time Huawei wanted to acquire or support domestic vendors, but after research found none were up to the task; domestic companies could only grow in the cracks of American giants, with small scale, weak R&D and weak product innovation. So Huawei decided to do it itself, benchmarking Oracle, investing 1 billion, 2 billion, 3 billion yuan a year starting in 2011 and 2012, without knowing whether there would be any output in the future.

points.h: The future is two centers, not one replacing the other
points.body: Fang Xingdong judges that global high tech moving from a single US-centered system to two centers is the general trend; politics will not allow a continued single center — the US will not allow it, and China will not allow it. He believes a single center is itself abnormal, and only two centers can create competition — only with two systems does every consumer, every company, every country, big or small, have a choice and not be forced to pick one side under coercion. So the mission of Huawei's six products is to go from being the second choice to being the better choice; it is not a simple substitution relationship with Nvidia but each having its strengths, complementing each other, and co-opetition. He admits the American system is currently stronger, with its advantage mainly in advanced manufacturing, and that Huawei, under process constraints, relies on the Tao Law to avoid being left behind; once advanced processes are also broken through, it can pursue both tracks at once.

points.h: The tech war won short term, but the long-term cost is greater
points.body: Fang Xingdong believes the US did indeed suppress Huawei through the tech war, but cannot solve the problem in the long term. He reasons: without the national confrontation of 2017 and 2018, Huawei might be at least one-third of Nvidia, one-third of Apple, possibly China's largest company by market cap; in 2019 Huawei had already surpassed Apple, and its global shipments briefly exceeded Samsung's for one quarter. Nvidia today is dominant; if it had been running neck and neck with Huawei in AI chips from the start, it could not have reached this position. He judges that once the attacked party builds a self-circulation that does not rely on the outside, and the other side cannot eliminate it even under the harshest conditions, it will be even harder to eliminate later; it will only grow stronger, turning from a monopoly into two competitors.

quotes.text: He said Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets harder and harder.
I have been in this industry for 30 years, and I feel that many of my past understandings can be reset to zero.
Without the tech war, Huawei is an excellent company, but it might not, would not become a great company; but with the tech war, it will definitely become a great company.

So Huawei's current hurdles are with technology, but in fact what it drives is the improvement of China's entire industry, the entire supply chain; but many things it has to do itself first, because if it does not do them, no one else can.
Once the attacked party, whether Huawei or China, builds a self-circulation, a self-circulation that does not rely on the outside, frankly speaking it becomes a long-term competitor.
